title: Stop running your dishwasher on hot dry
excerpt: Hot dry is the one setting almost everyone leaves on, and it's the reason your dishwasher door gasket looks ten years older than it is.
author: Elmir R.
content:
Most people never touch that setting. It ships with heated dry on, they run it that way for six years, and the first time they think about it is when I'm standing in their kitchen replacing a door gasket.

What that heating element is actually doing

After the final rinse, the heating element kicks on and holds the interior at roughly 140 to 145 degrees Fahrenheit for 30 to 45 minutes. That heat evaporates the water. It also works on every rubber seal, every plastic component, and every wire connection in the door assembly, every single cycle, for as long as you own the machine. It's not doing any of that damage dramatically. It's doing it slowly, cycle by cycle, in a way you won't notice until something fails.

The heating element itself has a finite number of high-heat cycles before resistance climbs and it starts drawing more current or fails outright. On machines where the same element handles water heating during the wash and then drying afterward, you're running it twice as hard. A replacement heating element on a mid-range KitchenAid or similar runs $45 to $85 for the part, plus about an hour of labor. That's a repair that shows up earlier than it should on machines where heated dry runs every cycle.

The gasket issue nobody mentions at purchase

Door gaskets are rubber. Rubber degrades faster with repeated heat exposure, and the failure pattern looks different from normal wear. Regular age compression gives you a gasket that's flattened and stiff. Heat fatigue gives you small lateral cracks, usually along the bottom corners, where the door flexes slightly every time it opens and closes. By the time those cracks are leaking, the customer has usually been running heated dry for five or more years and has no idea the two are connected.

I had a customer in Fairfield call us about her Whirlpool Gold from around 2018, slow seep onto the floor after every cycle. I pulled the gasket and it had exactly that heat-cracked look. I asked if she ran heated dry. She said yes, every cycle, because she thought air dry meant the dishes would smell. Gasket was $21. Labor was half an hour. She asked why the manual didn't say any of this. I told her it sort of does, buried in the fine print. They just don't make it obvious.

Bosch figured this out a long time ago

Bosch dishwashers don't use a traditional heating element for drying. They use condensation drying, which works by making the stainless steel tub cooler than the dishes so moisture migrates to the walls and drains away. No sustained high heat, no element cycling on after the rinse. Their tubs and gaskets age noticeably better than comparable Whirlpool or GE units, and I don't think that's a coincidence. When Bosch customers complain their dishes aren't "dry enough," they're usually comparing to a heated dry result from a previous machine. The dishes are dry. They're just not hot.

That engineering choice wasn't marketing. It was a straightforward answer to the wear problem heated dry creates.

The Whirlpool WDF board pattern

On Whirlpool's mid-tier WDF series dishwashers, I see a higher rate of control board failures when heated dry is combined with a heavy-cycle setting. The board is managing a long wash phase and then a sustained heating phase back to back, and that sustained load shortens its life. Control board replacements run $180 to $400 depending on the model. That's not a repair I enjoy quoting on a seven-year-old machine.

The energy math is straightforward

Heated dry adds roughly 15 to 20 cents per cycle in electricity. Run the dishwasher daily and that's around $55 to $70 a year, just for the drying phase. Over five years that's over $300, spent on accelerating the exact wear I described above. And you can get the same result for free by cracking the door open two inches at the end of the cycle and walking away for 20 minutes.

Plastic items will still have some water on them. That's physics, not a malfunction. Rinse aid handles most of it. A bottle of Finish Jet-Dry runs about $4 and lasts a couple of months. Honestly, that's the whole solution for most households.

One note on summer

In humid months, customers call us more often about dishes not drying properly even with heated dry running. Sometimes they respond by selecting a heavier cycle or making sure heated dry is set to "high." That usually makes things worse, not better. Humidity slows evaporation regardless of setting. Chasing dryness with more heat just adds wear. Open the door, let the steam out, done.

So here's what I'd tell you to do: go turn heated dry off today, buy a bottle of rinse aid if you don't use one, and start cracking the door at the end of the cycle. That's it. If you're already dealing with a leaking door or a dishwasher that's not finishing cycles correctly, contact our team and we'll tell you honestly whether it's worth fixing. If you already know you need someone out, go ahead and book a service call and we'll take a look.

title: Cleaning the lint trap isn't enough
excerpt: Most people clean the lint screen every load and think they're done. The part that actually causes fires is six inches behind it, and nobody touches it.
author: Elmir R.
content:
The lint screen catches maybe 70% of what your dryer produces. The rest, the fine particulate stuff that slips through the mesh, keeps moving. It coats the inside of the trap slot, sticks to the duct walls inside the cabinet, and packs itself into the blower wheel. After three to five years of regular use, that somewhere is full. And nobody cleaned it because nobody knew to look there.

Where lint actually goes after the screen

Airflow in a dryer runs drum to lint screen to blower wheel to exhaust duct. The screen is the first filter, not the last. Anything small enough to get past it rides the airstream straight into the blower housing. The blower wheel, which is the fan that actually pulls air through the machine, has fins designed to move air. Those same fins are perfect for catching fine lint. Over time they cake up, the wheel moves less air, and the dryer runs hotter and slower trying to compensate.

The trap slot itself is its own problem. Pull your lint screen out right now and look at the slot it lives in. Run your finger along the side walls. There's a felt-like gray layer built up in there, and it narrows the airflow opening whether or not your screen is spotless. A dryer lint brush, narrow and flexible, costs about $8 at any hardware store. That slot should get brushed out every three to six months. Most people do it never.

The blower wheel looks like a hamster wheel full of felt

I pulled a Whirlpool dryer out for a woman in Milford last year. She'd had her exhaust vent professionally cleaned six months before, so she ruled that out and figured the heating element was going. I pulled the back panel off, ran the machine for two minutes, and watched the blower wheel barely turn. It was so packed with lint it had almost no clearance. The heat was building up inside the cabinet because air had nowhere to go fast enough. I cleared the wheel, brushed out the slot, put the panel back on. She ran a full load of towels in 47 minutes. Parts: nothing. Her dryer had been limping along for almost a year, running two full cycles per load, because of an $8 brush job she didn't know to do.

Whirlpool and Maytag dryers from roughly 2015 to 2022 are the machines I open up most often with this problem. The exhaust path routing on those models pulls lint past the screen faster than some other designs. Samsung gas dryers from the same era show it too, sometimes faster. If I do ten dryer calls in a week, two or three of them trace back to internal lint restriction, not a failed component.

The thermal fuse that keeps blowing

On Whirlpool machines, the thermal fuse is part number 3392519. It costs about $6. It's a one-time safety device that cuts power to the heating circuit when the dryer gets too hot. When airflow is restricted by a packed blower wheel, temperatures inside the cabinet climb, and the fuse blows to protect the machine. That's the fuse doing exactly what it's supposed to do.

But here's the pattern I see constantly. Customer replaces the fuse, dryer works, fuse blows again four to six months later. They replace it again. Now they think the dryer is dying. It's not. The fuse is a symptom. The restricted airflow is the cause. Until you fix the airflow, you'll keep buying fuses.

What you can do yourself, and what you probably can't

The lint slot is a genuine DIY job. Pull the screen, grab a flexible lint brush, work it down both sides of the slot, and pull out whatever comes up. The first time you do this after a few years, you'll be surprised what the brush brings out. Do it twice a year going forward and it stays manageable.

The blower wheel is a different story. Getting to it usually means removing the front or rear panel depending on the brand, disconnecting a few wires, and knowing what you're looking at once you're in there. If you're comfortable with basic appliance disassembly, it's not complicated. If you're not, don't guess. A clogged blower on a machine that's otherwise fine is a $45 to $85 parts job if the wheel needs replacing, plus labor, and it's worth doing right. If you want someone to take a look, you can book a service call and we'll tell you honestly what we find.

One thing worth saying directly

Don't replace a heating element on a slow dryer until you've ruled out airflow restriction. A heating element on a standard electric dryer runs $30 to $55 in parts, and it's a reasonable fix when the element has actually failed. But a clogged blower mimics a bad element symptom-for-symptom: long drying times, clothes damp at the end of the cycle, heat that feels lower than it should. I've seen people spend money on a new element and have the exact same problem a month later because nobody looked at the blower.

The part didn't fix it. The airflow fixed it.

If your dryer has been running slow for more than a few months and a vent cleaning didn't solve it, contact our team or have someone pull the panel and check the blower before you buy anything. It's usually faster to diagnose than people expect.

If you're in Connecticut and want us to take a look, schedule a repair and we'll sort out what's actually going on.

title: Ice maker died again? It's probably not the ice maker.
excerpt: Most ice maker calls I go on, the ice maker itself is fine. The problem is almost always something upstream that nobody thinks to check.
author: Elmir R.
content:
Last spring I got a call from a guy in Branford who had already ordered a $200 ice maker assembly off Amazon. It was sitting on his counter in the box when I got there. The water inlet valve was clogged. He sent the assembly back unopened.

This is the most common version of this story. The ice maker gets blamed because it's the visible thing, the thing with a name, the thing that stopped doing its job. But the ice maker is usually the victim, not the cause.

The valve behind the fridge is the first place to look

The water inlet valve is a small electrically controlled valve that opens to let water into the ice maker. They wear out, they clog with mineral deposits, and when they fail the ice maker either cycles through its routine and produces nothing, or makes those thin hollow cubes that fall apart when you touch them. Valve replacement runs $40 to $80 in parts depending on the brand. That's a long way from a full ice maker assembly.

The symptoms can look identical. Ice maker runs, you hear it cycling, nothing comes out. People assume the module is dead. A lot of the time the module is fine and the valve isn't opening fully.

The filter nobody's touched in three years

Before you call anyone, go find your water filter. If you can't remember when you changed it last, change it now. A clogged filter creates enough flow restriction to starve the ice maker, and the ice maker just stops. No drama, no error code, just no ice.

I'd say half the people I talk to don't know where their filter is, or didn't know the fridge had one. Some of the in-door filter housings hide them pretty well. Most manufacturers say every six months. Realistically, once a year is fine for most households. Three years is not fine.

Freezer temperature does matter

Ice makers have a cutoff. If the freezer runs above roughly 10 degrees Fahrenheit, the ice maker shuts itself off. That's actually it working correctly, protecting itself from making a mess. So if your freezer is running warm because the evaporator fan is struggling or the door gasket has been leaking cold air for the last eight months, the ice maker isn't broken. It's just sitting there waiting for conditions that aren't coming.

Check your freezer temp with a cheap thermometer before assuming anything. If it's reading 18 or 20 degrees, the ice maker is the last thing you need to worry about.

Look at the line behind the fridge

This one takes ten minutes. Pull the fridge out and look at the water line. Kinked lines are more common than they should be, especially after someone slid the fridge back in a hurry. And in older houses where the kitchen plumbing runs near an exterior wall, that line can freeze in a bad winter. I've seen this in Waterbury a handful of times, usually in January. Thaws out, works fine, nobody ever knew.

When the ice maker itself is actually the problem

It does happen. The bail arm gets stuck in the off position, the mold thermostat fails, the motor burns out. If you need the full assembly replaced on a Samsung or Whirlpool, you're looking at $150 to $250 in parts plus labor. That's a reasonable fix on a fridge that's under eight or ten years old. On a fifteen-year-old unit, the conversation gets more complicated, and I'll tell you that honestly when you call.

You can take a look at our appliance repair services to get a sense of what we cover, and if you want a straight answer about whether something's worth fixing, just contact our team and we'll tell you what we think before you spend anything.

But do the easy stuff first. Filter, temperature, water line. Half the time you've already fixed it before anyone shows up. If you haven't, schedule a repair and we'll start with the valve, not the part you already ordered off Amazon.

title: Stacking your washer and dryer is probably voiding your warranty
excerpt: Stacking your washer and dryer without the right kit can void your warranty and destroy drum bearings fast. Here's what Connecticut homeowners need to know.
author: Elmir R.
content:
Last spring I got a call out to Naugatuck — a couple in a condo who'd been stacking their laundry for two years on a piece of plywood they'd cut to fit. Front-load washer on the bottom, top-load dryer sitting on top. I'm not joking about the plywood. The dryer drum was so worn out of round I could see it wobbling through the door glass. They had no idea any of this was connected to how they'd set the machines up.

This is more common than I'd like to admit. Not always the plywood, but the general situation — people stacking their washer and dryer without thinking too hard about it, assuming that if it physically fits, it's fine. It's not fine. And beyond the mechanical damage, it may already be costing you a warranty claim you don't know you've lost yet.

Why so many people end up stacking in the first place

Laundry closets. Finished basements with low ceilings. Condos where the builder gave you thirty-six inches of floor space and called it a laundry room. Stacking is just the obvious move when you're working with a tight footprint, and appliance manufacturers know this — which is exactly why they make stacking kits. They'd rather sell you the kit than have you rig something up.

Most people skip the kit entirely. Or they buy a generic shelf-style bracket they found online for twelve dollars. Or they do the plywood thing. The manufacturer's stacking kit for most Whirlpool and LG front-loaders runs somewhere between thirty and sixty dollars depending on where you source it. It's designed specifically to lock the dryer to the washer frame so vibration doesn't transfer the way it otherwise would. That's the whole job the kit does. It's not complicated, but skipping it is how you turn a five-year-old dryer into a three-year-old dryer.

The mechanical damage from improper stacking

Whirlpool and LG are the two brands I see this on the most, partly because their stacking requirements are buried deep in the installation manual — not on the first page, not on a sticker on the unit. You have to go looking. So people don't find it, they stack the washer and dryer without the kit, and six months later the dryer starts making a low rumble that slowly gets worse.

What's happening is the spin cycle on the washer sends vibration up into the dryer. Without the kit creating a rigid connection, the dryer just absorbs that energy through its feet. Over time this accelerates wear on the drum bearings. I've also seen it travel into the dryer's control board — twice in the last year I diagnosed a control board failure and traced it directly back to vibration from an improperly stacked setup. Control boards are a much more expensive problem than drum bearings.

None of this requires a dramatic failure to be doing damage. It's slow, cumulative wear that shows up on a service call two years later and looks like a random breakdown.

Leveling matters more when the units are stacked

One unlevel unit throws off both of them. I say this on basically every stacked-setup call I go on. People level the bottom unit, set the dryer on top, and assume they're done. But the stacking kit and the leveling legs work together. If the whole column is slightly off, the washer rocks during spin, the dryer rocks with it, and now you've got two machines doing something they shouldn't be doing.

Check the level after you install the kit. Both units — not just the washer.

The warranty part nobody expects

Here's where it gets genuinely frustrating. Most major brands will ask about installation before honoring a warranty claim on a washer or dryer — how it's set up, whether it's stacked, what kit was used. "Improper installation" is a real denial reason, and stacking a washer and dryer without the correct manufacturer-approved kit qualifies.

I had a customer in Meriden who'd paid for an extended warranty on both her machines. She called me after two previous repair visits from someone else hadn't solved a rattling problem. Turned out the washer was shaking the entire column and the dryer was showing the symptoms. The extended warranty had already denied one claim. She was on her own by the time I got there.

She'd bought that warranty in good faith. Paid real money for it. And the improper stacking setup had voided her coverage before anything ever went wrong. Nobody told her that at the store.

If you're already stacked, here's what to actually do

Don't panic — most situations are fixable. Here's the order I recommend:

  • Confirm your models are rated to stack together. Not all front-loaders are, even within the same brand, and mixing brands is almost always a problem. The model numbers are on a sticker inside the door frame. Look them up, find the installation guide, and check stacking compatibility. This takes ten minutes and it matters.
  • Get the right manufacturer-approved stacking kit. Appliance parts suppliers usually carry them. At MY APPLIANCE Repair we can typically source the correct kit within a day or two. You can see more about our appliance repair services if you're not sure what you're dealing with.
  • Re-level both units from scratch after the kit goes in. Don't assume the floor is doing the work. Adjust the leveling legs on the washer first, then confirm the dryer is plumb at the top of the stack.
  • Listen for anything new. If a noise started right after stacking, something was likely already worn before the stack went up. Don't wait — book a service call before the problem reaches parts that cost real money.

One situation where unstacking is the right answer

If one of your machines is significantly older than the other, think hard before stacking a new unit on top of a worn-out one. A washer that's already vibrating more than it should — because the drum bearings are going or the shock absorbers are tired — is going to punish whatever's sitting on top of it.

In cases like that, the honest recommendation is to unstack, address the worn machine, and then re-stack correctly with the proper kit. It costs more upfront but it's cheaper than replacing a dryer control board six months from now.

Get a stacked laundry setup checked by a Connecticut repair tech

If any of this sounds like your setup, MY APPLIANCE Repair services Naugatuck, Meriden, and communities throughout Connecticut. It usually takes about ten minutes on-site to tell you whether the stack is the problem — and most of the time we can source the right stacking kit and correct the installation in the same visit.

Book a service call online, or contact our team if you have questions before scheduling. We'd rather help you get the setup right than come back later for a drum bearing job.

title: Leaving food in your fridge when the power goes out costs you more than you think
excerpt: A closed refrigerator stays safe for 4 hours during a power outage — only if you stop opening it. What to keep, toss, and how to protect your fridge.
author: Elmir R.
content:
A woman in Meriden called us after a storm last spring. Power had been out for about eight hours, and she'd opened the fridge maybe five or six times to check on things. "Just a quick look," she kept saying. She lost everything in there — and honestly, with a little power outage refrigerator food safety knowledge, she didn't have to lose any of it.

That call happens more than you'd think. So here's what the team at MY APPLIANCE Repair tells people standing in their kitchen the day after a storm — because it saves food, and sometimes it saves your compressor.

How long your refrigerator actually stays safe during a power outage

The four-hour window

A closed refrigerator holds a safe temperature for roughly four hours during a power outage. A packed freezer can hold it for a full day or two. The word that matters in both of those sentences is closed.

Every time you open the door you're letting cold air fall out and warm air pour in. It's not dramatic — it just adds up fast. Five "quick looks" over eight hours and you've blown the whole window. The fridge can't tell you whether your leftovers are okay by you staring at them. A thermometer can. Most people don't own one. A basic refrigerator thermometer runs about six dollars and is worth having before you need it.

If the outage is going to run long

If it looks like power won't be back within a few hours, move what matters most into a cooler with ice before the four-hour mark — don't wait until after. Prioritize:

  • Deli meat and opened packages of poultry or fish
  • Opened dairy — milk, cream, soft cheeses
  • Anything already cooked
  • Items with eggs or mayo

Leave condiments where they are. More on that below.

Refrigerator food safety: what to actually throw out

The rule for power outage refrigerator food safety is 40°F. If your fridge has been above that temperature for more than two hours, certain things have to go. No exceptions:

  • Cooked meat, poultry, and fish
  • Cut fruit and leafy greens
  • Soft cheeses and opened dairy
  • Anything with eggs in it — casseroles, quiche, custards
  • Opened mayo and creamy dressings
  • Leftover takeout

Condiments are more forgiving than people think. Ketchup, mustard, pickles, hard cheeses, butter, and whole fruits and vegetables are not the things that get you sick. It's cooked proteins and dairy-heavy items you need to be honest about.

If you don't have a thermometer and you're guessing — that's exactly what it is. A guess. Food poisoning from spoiled chicken is not a fun way to spend a Tuesday.

Freezer food safety after a power outage

Everyone asks the same thing: "Is it still frozen?" And they want the answer to be yes. The real question is whether it partially thawed and refroze, because that's what actually causes problems.

  • Safe: Meat that's still cold and firm all the way to the center.
  • Discard: Anything soft in the middle, or with visible pooled liquid in the bag — that refroze.

Ice crystals on the surface don't tell you much. "Still has some ice on it" is not the same as "safe to eat." The freezer is more forgiving than the fridge during a power outage, but it has limits too.

The fridge damage that shows up two days later

This is the part no food safety guide covers, because they're not written by appliance technicians. Power coming back isn't always gentle. Voltage spikes on restore hit your refrigerator's electrical components hard — especially the start relay and the control board.

We got a call in Waterbury last winter, two days after a big storm. Three-year-old Samsung, completely dead. Compressor not running, not cold. The customer had a surge protector on his TV, his router, his gaming setup — nothing on the fridge. The control board was fried. That was a $280 repair. A decent surge protector for an appliance outlet runs about $25.

Parts most likely to fail after a power outage

  • Start relay: $40–$80 for the part. One of the most common failures we see after outage events.
  • Control board: $200 or more on newer Samsung and LG units with advanced electronics.
  • Compressor: Less common, but voltage irregularities on restore can stress it over time.

If your refrigerator is plugged into a plain wall outlet with no surge protection right now, that's the single easiest thing you can change before the next storm.

What to do after the power comes back

Give the compressor time to stabilize

Wait 15 to 20 minutes before loading food back into the refrigerator. Let the compressor cycle up and stabilize. Listen for it — a healthy compressor starts up, runs for a bit, then goes quiet. It should do that several times in the first hour.

Signs something is wrong

If the compressor is running constantly and the temperature isn't dropping, that's a problem. Either the compressor is struggling or something in the sealed system took damage. Watch the temp over the next two to three hours. If it's not back down to the mid-30s by then, stop loading food into it and call someone.

At MY APPLIANCE Repair, we're happy to help you figure out what you're dealing with before you commit to a service visit. Contact our team and describe what you're hearing — we can usually tell you over the phone whether it warrants a visit or whether the unit just needs more time to recover. We'd rather spend two minutes on a call than have you throw out another fridge full of food unnecessarily.

Before the next storm: a short checklist

  • Put a $6 refrigerator thermometer inside your fridge today
  • Plug your refrigerator into a surge-protected outlet
  • Keep a cooler and ice packs on hand during storm season
  • Resist the urge to open the door during an outage

Connecticut storm season runs from spring thunderstorms straight through to nor'easters in late fall. A little preparation on power outage refrigerator food safety genuinely makes a difference. If you want to know more about what we handle, take a look at our appliance repair services.

If your refrigerator is acting up after a recent power outage — not cooling, running constantly, or completely dead — don't wait to see if it works itself out. Book a service call with MY APPLIANCE Repair and we'll come take a look. Better to catch a start relay early than replace a control board later.

title: Refrigerators die younger than they used to, and here's why
excerpt: Refrigerators built in the last decade fail years sooner than older models — here's why, and what Connecticut homeowners can do about it.
author: Elmir R.
content:
The "they don't make 'em like they used to" thing is usually nostalgia talking. With refrigerators, it's actually true, and I say that as someone who does refrigerator repair for a living — not as someone who's bitter about progress.

Had a call in Naugatuck about six weeks ago. Samsung side-by-side, seven years old, second compressor failure. The couple who owned it kept asking what they were doing wrong. Nothing. They were doing nothing wrong. The machine just isn't built with the same margin for error that older units were.

What actually changed in modern refrigerator design

Modern fridges run inverter compressors, which are more efficient but more sensitive — especially to voltage fluctuations and heat. Manufacturers also thinned out the insulation to hit energy efficiency ratings. Tighter tolerances, less buffer. And there are more electronics now: control boards, thermistors, door sensors, ice maker modules. Every one of those is a failure point that didn't exist on a 1994 Whirlpool top-freezer that's still running in someone's garage right now.

French door and bottom-freezer designs put the compressor down near the floor, where it's warmer and where dust and pet hair collect faster. That matters more than people think, and it's one of the first things we check on a refrigerator repair call.

The brands we see most often on service calls

We're not here to trash anyone, but we'd be doing you a disservice if we didn't say this: Samsung sealed system failures and LG linear compressor failures are something the team at MY APPLIANCE Repair sees constantly across Connecticut. The LG linear compressor issue is well-documented in the trade. A lot of those units are dying at five or six years old. We've seen it enough times that when someone calls with a newer LG French door that stopped cooling, we already have a pretty good idea what we're walking into.

Older GE and Whirlpool top-freezers from the nineties? Still running. Newer versions of those same brands are a different story too, though not quite as bad in our experience.

Refrigerator maintenance you can actually control

Most refrigerator problems we see in Connecticut homes could have been delayed — or avoided — with a few simple habits. Here's what makes the biggest difference:

Simple steps that extend your fridge's life

  • Clean the condenser coils once a year. They're under the fridge or behind it, depending on the model. It takes ten minutes and a vacuum. Dust and pet hair make the compressor work harder and run hotter, shortening its life. This is the single most skipped maintenance item we see.
  • Check your door gasket. Close the door on a dollar bill and pull it out. You should feel resistance. If it slides right out, the gasket is soft and your compressor is running constantly trying to compensate.
  • Don't install it with zero clearance. Counter-depth and built-in setups look great, but if heat has nowhere to go, you're slowly cooking the compressor. The manual has clearance specs for a reason.
  • Don't wait if it's running warm. If it's running all the time and the inside is warm, call someone soon. The food loss will cost you more than the repair if you wait two weeks.

The repair-or-replace question

Here's roughly how we talk through it with customers. Compressor replacement on a newer unit runs $400 to $600 in parts and labor, sometimes more on sealed systems. If the fridge is under seven years old and the compressor's gone, that's a real conversation about whether to repair or replace. If it's over ten years old and needs a control board — which usually runs $150 to $250 — we'd almost always fix it. Our general rule: if the refrigerator repair costs more than half of what a comparable new fridge costs, think hard before saying yes.

Had a couple in Cheshire last spring with a six-year-old LG French door, linear compressor gone. They'd bought the extended warranty and it covered most of it. Honestly, extended warranties on refrigerators are one of the few times we think they actually make sense, given where the industry is right now. For most appliances we'd tell you to skip it. Fridges are the exception.

What to do if yours is already struggling

If your refrigerator is running constantly, not holding temperature, or making noises it didn't used to make, don't sit on it. The longer a compressor runs under stress, the more it costs to fix — and at some point the repair window closes entirely. Connecticut homeowners who call early almost always spend less.

You can take a look at our appliance repair services or contact our team and describe what it's doing. Half the time the MY APPLIANCE Repair team can narrow it down before we even show up at your door.

None of this is doom and gloom. It's just: know what you bought, do the simple maintenance, and don't be surprised if a 2019 fridge needs work. It's not you.

If something's already wrong, go ahead and book a service call and we'll take a look. Sooner is usually cheaper.

title: Your oven's self-clean cycle is doing more harm than good
excerpt: The oven self-clean cycle hits 900°F and regularly kills control boards, fuses, and door locks. Here's when to skip it — and what to do instead.
author: Elmir R.
content:
Every fall I start bracing for it. Sometime around the third week of October, people remember the holidays are coming, look inside their oven, and decide to run the self-clean cycle. By Thanksgiving week I'm fielding calls from homeowners whose oven is locked shut, throwing an error code, with twenty people coming to dinner the next day.

It happens almost every year across Connecticut — Meriden, Middletown, New Haven, you name it. And honestly, it's predictable, because the oven self-clean cycle is one of the roughest things you can put a residential range through.

What the self-clean cycle is actually doing in there

Self-clean locks the door and cranks the oven up to somewhere around 900 degrees Fahrenheit — sometimes higher — and holds it there for two to four hours. The idea is that the heat incinerates whatever's baked onto the walls and floor, and you wipe out the ash when it's done. In theory, fine. In practice, you're running an oven that normally lives at 350 to 400 degrees at more than twice that temperature for hours at a stretch.

The electronics don't love that. Neither do the mechanical parts. That combination is why the oven self-clean cycle generates more repair calls than almost any other single feature on a range.

What actually breaks — and why

There are three failure points that come up over and over on self-clean-related service calls:

Thermal fuse failure

The thermal fuse goes first most often. It's a safety cutoff designed to trip if the oven gets dangerously hot — which is exactly what the oven self-clean cycle does by design. When the fuse blows, the oven just stops working. The part itself is cheap, usually fifteen to thirty dollars, but labor to diagnose and access it pushes the total repair cost higher than most people expect.

Control board failure

Control board failures are the ones that really sting. I see this consistently on LG ranges and on newer Frigidaires — models from roughly 2017 onward. The board sits in a spot where heat accumulates during the cycle, and on an oven that's already eight or ten years old, the components aren't as tolerant as they once were. I had a GE range in Meriden last spring where the owner ran the self-clean cycle, the board fried partway through, and the repair estimate came out to more than she wanted to spend on an oven that age. Bad outcome for a feature she was using to take care of the appliance.

Door lock mechanism failure

Door lock mechanisms jam or fail too. The lock has to engage before the cycle starts and release after the oven cools down, and that mechanism takes real abuse over time. When it sticks mid-cycle, the door won't open — even after the oven is completely cold. I've talked people through waiting it out, cycling the breaker, all of it. Sometimes it works. Sometimes I'm driving over there.

To summarize what the oven self-clean cycle regularly breaks:

  • Thermal fuse — trips from the extreme heat; oven goes completely dead
  • Control board — heat exposure degrades components, especially on ranges 7+ years old
  • Door lock mechanism — jams engaged, trapping you out of the oven until it releases or is serviced

The timing problem makes all of this worse

People run the self-clean cycle right before they need the oven. The cycle takes three to four hours plus a cool-down period before the door will unlock, so you're committing a big chunk of your day. If something goes wrong mid-cycle, you have no oven, a locked door, and no good options. Running it the night before Thanksgiving is genuinely one of the riskier things you can do in your kitchen.

The fix is simple: if you're going to run it at all, do it on a low-stakes day — not the week of a holiday, not the night before a dinner party, and not on an oven that's already showing age.

When it's actually reasonable to use it

If your oven is newer — three or four years old — and you've got light buildup rather than a year's worth of baked-on grease, running the oven self-clean cycle once a year probably isn't going to cause problems. But follow these ground rules:

  • Do it on a day when you can go without the oven entirely if something goes sideways
  • Never run it the night before you need it
  • Don't run it when the oven is heavily soiled — more material to burn means more heat and smoke on top of what the cycle already generates
  • Don't run it every few months the way some people do

Once a year, light soil, plenty of time. That's about the best-case scenario.

What to do instead

Baking soda and a little dish soap. Make a paste, spread it on the dirty surfaces, let it sit for twenty minutes, then scrub it out. Takes some elbow grease but it works, it won't fry a two-hundred-dollar control board, and you can still use your oven that same day. I tell this to roughly half the customers I talk to about oven maintenance. A good number of them look at me like I'm nuts because they paid for the self-clean feature and feel like they should use it. I get that. But you also paid for the control board, and replacing it isn't fun.

If you want to know more about what we handle on service calls, take a look at our appliance repair services. If something already went wrong, contact our team and we'll figure out what happened.

The short version: the oven self-clean cycle isn't going to destroy a newer range used occasionally and carefully. But running it on an older oven the week of a holiday is exactly how MY APPLIANCE Repair ends up at your house on a bad night. Don't be that call. Clean it by hand this time.

If you're already dealing with an oven that won't heat, won't unlock, or threw an error code mid-cycle, book a service call and we'll get out to you. MY APPLIANCE Repair serves homeowners throughout Connecticut — it's always better to know what you're dealing with than to wait and hope.

title: Stop unplugging your appliances during a storm
excerpt: Yanking cords mid-strike can damage a control board faster than the surge itself. What Connecticut homeowners should do instead — and when.
author: Elmir R.
content:
Unplugging appliances during a storm sounds like the responsible move. It's advice Connecticut homeowners have been passing around for decades. But the timing and the method are the parts nobody talks about — and getting them wrong has cost some of our customers real money.

The timing is everything. If you're yanking cords out of the wall while lightning is already striking nearby, you're not protecting anything. You're pulling a disconnect at exactly the moment a voltage spike might be traveling through the line. That's the worst possible window. The arc risk alone should give you pause.

The right move is before the storm. Watch the forecast, and if there's a thunderstorm warning for the evening, unplug your sensitive appliances in the afternoon. That's the whole strategy for safely unplugging appliances during a storm.

If you missed that window, leave everything alone

Seriously. If the storm is already on top of you and you didn't unplug anything beforehand, just let it ride. If you have a surge protector on your TV or computer, let it do its job. If you don't have one, that's a problem to solve next week. Unplugging appliances during a storm that's already active is not the answer — it can introduce its own damage.

We had a call out of Naugatuck a couple of years back that we still think about. A customer heard thunder, panicked, and yanked the washing machine cord mid-rinse cycle. The machine never got hit by lightning — the surge didn't even reach it. But killing power mid-cycle scrambled the control board anyway. That was a $280 repair, completely avoidable.

Not every appliance deserves the same treatment

When you do have time to unplug before a storm, prioritize in this order:

  • Unplug first: TVs, computers, and microwaves with digital displays. The control boards inside are sensitive and expensive to replace. A fried board in a mid-range microwave can cost more to fix than the microwave is worth.
  • Leave running: Your refrigerator. Unplugging it mid-storm creates problems beyond food safety. Compressors don't love being cut and restarted abruptly. We've had customers unplug their fridge "to be safe," plug it back in right after the storm, and call us convinced the fridge was dead. It wasn't — the compressor just needed a few minutes to equalize pressure before it would kick on.
  • Use judgment on: Washers and dryers. If a cycle is running, stopping it abruptly carries its own risks, as the Naugatuck story above shows.

If the fridge is running, leave it running.

What your surge protector probably can't handle

Most of what people call surge protectors are just power strips. There's a real difference. A true surge protector has a joule rating printed on the box — most homeowners have never heard of one. If you can't find that rating, assume the strip isn't doing much beyond adding outlets.

Point-of-use strips rated 1,000 joules or above are worth having for electronics. For appliances — especially anything running a digital control board — the better investment is whole-house surge protection installed at the panel. An electrician can put one in for roughly $300 to $500 depending on your setup. It covers everything at once and handles spikes that would blow right through a cheap strip.

Modern appliances are genuinely more vulnerable to surges than machines from twenty years ago. The old mechanical washers didn't have much to fry. Today's equipment is running software. A bad storm season a few years back brought the team at MY APPLIANCE Repair a stretch of LG French door refrigerators with fried main boards, one after another. Those repairs were landing between $350 and $500 — exactly the range where the conversation about repair versus replacement gets genuinely uncomfortable. You can browse our appliance repair services to get a sense of what we typically handle, but trust us: you'd rather not be in that conversation.

When the storm clears, don't flip everything back on at once

Stagger your restarts. Give the grid a minute to stabilize, then bring things back on in sequence:

  1. Refrigerator first
  2. Washer and dryer
  3. Everything else

If the fridge doesn't kick on right away, wait ten minutes before assuming anything is wrong. Compressors need a pressure equalization period after being off. Most of the panicked post-storm calls MY APPLIANCE Repair receives resolve themselves before we're even in the truck.

A note for older Connecticut homes

If your Connecticut home has older wiring, surges travel through it more easily. It's a strong reason to take the whole-house protector idea seriously — and to be especially careful about unplugging appliances during a storm incorrectly. Older wiring doesn't absorb or dissipate spikes the way modern installations can.

Late spring through early fall is when storm damage to appliances peaks across Connecticut, so now is a reasonable time to think it through rather than react badly when the sky goes dark.

If something did take a hit and you're not sure what you're dealing with, contact our team and we'll tell you honestly whether it's worth repairing. If you already know you need service, go ahead and book a service call and we'll get out to you. We're usually a few days out, but we move fast on anything keeping food from staying cold.

title: That clicking noise from your fridge is almost never random
excerpt: A refrigerator clicking noise in your Connecticut home usually means a failing start relay or defrost problem — and waiting even a few days can turn an $18 fix into a $600 repair.
author: Elmir R.
content:
That clicking noise from your fridge is almost never random

Three weeks. That's how long a guy in Branford had been hearing a soft click from his fridge every few minutes before he finally called MY APPLIANCE Repair. He figured it was the icemaker doing something weird, or maybe just the house settling. It wasn't. The start relay had failed, the compressor was hot to the touch when I got there, and he was about two or three days from a $600+ repair instead of an $18 part. We caught it. But barely.

A refrigerator clicking noise is the call I get more than almost any other. Some noise, some waiting, and then either a lucky catch or an expensive lesson. So let me walk you through what the different clicks actually mean — because they're not all the same, and some of them genuinely can't wait.

That marble-rattling sound near the bottom of the fridge

If you hear a click or a rattling shake every few minutes — usually from the lower back area — and your fridge isn't keeping things as cold as it used to, that's almost certainly the start relay. It's a small part that helps kick the compressor on. When it fails, the compressor tries to start, can't, and gives up. Then tries again. That refrigerator clicking noise you're hearing is the compressor cycling through failed start attempts. The relay itself is $10 to $25 and is an easy replacement.

Here's the thing, though. Sometimes the relay failed because the compressor was already working too hard — already running hot, already struggling. The relay is the canary. So when I replace a relay, I'm also checking whether the compressor itself is in decent shape, because if it's not, we're having a different conversation.

I had a woman in Naugatuck two months ago who was convinced it was the icemaker. She'd been googling icemaker noises for a week. It was the relay the whole time. The icemaker was fine. Took me about twenty minutes total.

The click that happens on a schedule

Different sound, different location, different rhythm. If you notice a clicking or a soft thunk that seems to happen roughly every eight to twelve hours, that's usually the defrost cycle kicking in or off. Your fridge runs a defrost cycle automatically to melt frost that builds up on the evaporator coils inside the freezer section. It's supposed to do this. The click you're hearing is often the defrost timer or the heater relay switching states.

Normal, mostly. But if you're also seeing frost building up on your freezer walls, or the fridge section is warmer than it should be, or food is freezing unevenly, the defrost system isn't completing the cycle properly. Left alone, you get a full frost blockage over the evaporator — airflow stops, temperatures climb, and the repair goes from an $80 timer to a full evaporator replacement and significantly more labor. The click was telling you something. It's worth acting on before the frost wins.

Sounds like a playing card in a bicycle wheel

Intermittent, kind of rhythmic, coming from the back or underneath — that's usually the condenser fan hitting something. A piece of debris, a warped blade, occasionally a wire that's vibrated loose into the fan's path. This one is annoying but usually cheap if you deal with it quickly. If you let the fan motor run against resistance long enough, the motor burns out. Now it's a $120 to $180 part plus labor instead of five minutes clearing debris.

Pull the fridge out from the wall and look. You don't need to call anyone just to look.

Icemaker and compressor clicks: what's the difference?

Normal icemaker sounds

People confuse compressor-area sounds with icemaker sounds constantly. It's hard to localize noise in a kitchen. The icemaker has its own clicking and cycling sounds that are almost always normal: a click when it harvests ice, a buzz when it calls for water, some clunking when cubes drop. These are not the sounds to worry about.

If the icemaker is clicking repeatedly without making ice, that's usually a water inlet valve issue — annoying and fixable, but not urgent in the same way as a compressor-related refrigerator clicking noise.

The hard thump at startup, and then nothing

This one is the serious one. A loud clunk when the fridge tries to start, followed by silence, followed by the fridge not running at all — or running but not cooling — can be the compressor itself hard-starting or failing to start. At that point you're looking at $300 to $500 or more for a compressor job, and the honest conversation becomes whether that investment makes sense for the age and brand of the fridge.

Here's what I tell customers in their kitchens: if the fridge is under eight years old and not one of the brands I keep seeing relay failures on around the five-to-seven-year mark, a compressor repair usually makes sense. If it's twelve years old and already had one repair, I'm going to be straight with you about where that money goes.

Why Connecticut summers make refrigerator clicking noise worse

A start relay that was limping through March will often quit in July. Connecticut kitchens get warm, and when ambient temperatures rise, your compressor works harder to maintain the set temperature. Marginal parts — a relay already on its way out, a condenser fan already struggling — don't survive heat waves. If you've been meaning to call about a noise for a few weeks, summer is genuinely the worst time to keep waiting.

This is especially true in older homes without central air, which we see a lot of in towns like New Haven, Waterbury, Meriden, and Branford. A kitchen that hits 85°F in August puts real stress on a refrigeration system that was already sending you warning clicks.

Quick triage: how urgent is your refrigerator clicking noise?

Use this to judge how fast you need to act:

  • Clicking + fridge not cooling: Call today. Food is at risk and something is already failing.
  • Clicking every few minutes from the bottom: Likely the start relay. Don't wait more than a day or two.
  • Rhythmic click every 8–12 hours, fridge cooling normally: Monitor it, but schedule a look soon.
  • Fan-area rattle, everything else fine: Pull the fridge out and check for debris. If you can't find it, call us.
  • Loud thump at startup + no cooling: Stop using the fridge and call immediately.

Common questions Connecticut homeowners ask

Is a clicking refrigerator dangerous?

A clicking fridge is rarely a safety hazard in the immediate sense, but a failing compressor or start relay can overheat and accelerate food spoilage. When clicking is paired with warmth inside the fridge, treat it as urgent.

How much does it cost to fix a clicking refrigerator in Connecticut?

Most refrigerator clicking noise repairs fall between $75 and $250 depending on the cause. A start relay replacement is typically on the low end. A defrost system repair or compressor job will cost more, which is exactly why catching it early matters.

What brands see the most start relay problems?

In our service area, we see a disproportionate number of relay failures in certain LG and Samsung models at the five-to-seven-year mark. If you have one of those and you're hearing clicking, don't dismiss it.

Ready to stop guessing? Book a repair today.

If your fridge is clicking and also not cooling well, don't wait. You can book a service call right now — MY APPLIANCE Repair is typically able to get out to Connecticut customers within a day or two.

Not sure how urgent it is? Contact our team and describe what you're hearing. We can usually give you a rough sense of urgency before I'm even at your door. A pattern — when it clicks, how often, whether it changed recently — helps me diagnose faster and saves you time on the visit.

title: Why Your Washing Machine Shakes, Walks, and Bangs: Connecticut's Uneven Floor Problem and What It's Costing You
excerpt: Washing machine vibration in Connecticut homes is more than annoying — it destroys drum bearings and floods basements. Here's how to fix it fast.
author: Elmir R.
content:
Your washing machine shakes. It bangs. Maybe it's slowly migrating across the laundry room floor like it has somewhere better to be. Washing machine vibration is one of the most common appliance complaints we hear from Connecticut homeowners — and it's also one of the most misunderstood. If you've chalked it up to an old machine or just the way things are, you're likely underestimating what it's costing you. Excessive washing machine vibration isn't something to ignore, and in Connecticut homes specifically, it tends to be worse, more damaging, and more expensive than homeowners realize.

It's Not Just Annoying — It's Expensive

Vibration is one of the leading causes of premature washing machine failure. Every spin cycle that sends your machine rattling transfers stress directly to the components keeping it running. Drum bearings — the parts that allow the drum to spin smoothly — take the worst of it. When they fail, you're looking at $200–$400 or more in parts and labor. That's assuming the drum spider arm hasn't failed too, which is a separate repair entirely.

There's also a flooding risk that Connecticut homeowners with finished basements need to take seriously. Vibration gradually works water supply hose connections loose. Over dozens of cycles, that slight loosening becomes a slow drip — or, eventually, a burst connection mid-cycle. If your laundry area sits above a finished basement, the water damage bill can dwarf any appliance repair cost many times over. At My Appliance Repair, we see this scenario regularly in CT homes, and it's almost always traced back to washing machine vibration that went unaddressed for too long.

Why Connecticut Homes Are Especially Vulnerable

Connecticut has one of the oldest housing stocks in the nation. Colonials, Cape Cods, split-levels, raised ranches — most were built well before 1970, when subfloor construction methods, materials, and load expectations were very different. Aged hardwood and softwood subfloors flex and compress unevenly over decades. What was a flat, stable surface in 1955 may have shifted, settled, and warped considerably by now.

Many Connecticut homeowners have also added laundry in spaces that were never designed for it — finished basements, mudroom additions, second-floor closets carved out during renovations. These spaces weren't engineered with appliance loads in mind, and that matters. A washing machine in high-speed spin can reach 1,200–1,600 RPM. That's a significant dynamic load on residential floor joists that were built to support furniture and foot traffic, not machinery.

Second-floor laundry is increasingly popular in CT new builds and gut renovations — and it amplifies vibration dramatically. The energy travels straight through the joists and into the structure of the house. Fairfield County and New Haven County homeowners in older Victorian and Colonial homes face particular risk, where original hardwood sits over plank subfloor construction with little to dampen the transmission.

There's also a seasonal factor worth mentioning. Connecticut winters are cold and dry, and wood subfloors contract slightly as humidity drops. That subtle dimensional change can affect how your machine's feet contact the floor, making washing machine vibration noticeably worse in January than it was in September. It's a real effect, even if it sounds minor.

The Four Real Causes of Washing Machine Vibration

1. Uneven or Unlevel Feet

This is the number one cause. All four feet must make solid, even contact with the floor. Most machines have self-leveling rear feet, but they only work correctly if the machine is positioned and front-leveled properly first. If one foot is floating even slightly, the machine rocks during spin and the vibration compounds with every rotation.

2. Unbalanced Loads

A single heavy item — a comforter, a pair of jeans, a thick towel — can clump to one side of the drum during spin and throw the whole machine off balance. Newer machines pause and attempt to redistribute the load automatically, but older machines push straight through, hammering the drum suspension with every revolution.

3. Worn Drum Bearings, Spider Arms, or Shock Absorbers

If your vibration has gotten progressively worse over several months, this is the red flag. Worn bearings produce a low rumbling or grinding sound during spin. Worn shock absorbers and suspension rods are sneakier — they wear out silently and are often the hidden culprit in machines five or more years old. Combined with Connecticut's hard water, which accelerates bearing corrosion, these components can fail faster than the national average. (We covered how hard water damages appliances in a recent post — worth a read if you haven't seen it.)

4. Shipping Bolts Left In

Surprisingly common after a move or a used machine purchase. Shipping bolts lock the drum in place for transport — if they're never removed, the suspension system can't function at all. If you recently moved or bought a secondhand machine and it's violently loud during spin, check for shipping bolts before anything else.

DIY Fixes That Actually Work

Before calling a technician, there are a few things worth trying yourself:

  • Level the machine properly. Place a bubble level on top of the machine front-to-back and side-to-side. Adjust the front feet by hand — they thread in and out — until the bubble centers. Lock the jam nuts tight against the machine body so the feet can't drift. For rear self-leveling feet, use the tilt-and-drop method: tip the machine forward slightly onto its front feet, then lower it back down. The rear feet will reset to the floor automatically.
  • Add anti-vibration pads. Rubber composite pads outperform foam ones significantly. They won't fix a mechanical problem, but they do reduce vibration transmission to your floor and can make a real difference in homes with hardwood or older subfloors. Fairfield and New Haven County homeowners especially — these are worth the $30–$50 investment.
  • Balance your loads. Redistribute laundry manually when the machine pauses mid-cycle. Avoid washing single heavy items alone — add a few towels to balance the drum. For small or tangled items, use a mesh laundry bag to keep things even.
  • Check the subfloor itself. If you notice visible bounce when walking near the machine, or cracking grout on adjacent tile, the subfloor may be flexing under load. That's a contractor conversation, not a washing machine conversation.

The Second-Floor Laundry Warning for Connecticut Homeowners

If your laundry is on the second floor and the washing machine vibration is severe, pay attention to what's happening in the room below. Cracking drywall on the ceiling, doors nearby that have stopped closing properly, or visible flex in the ceiling when the machine runs — these are signs of structural stress, not just an appliance issue. A stacked washer/dryer unit actually reduces vibration transfer compared to a side-by-side pair in a tight closet, so if you're renovating, that's worth factoring into your layout decisions. For serious second-floor vibration concerns, a structural contractor should weigh in alongside any appliance repair work.

When DIY Isn't Enough: Signs You Need a Repair Technician

Some vibration problems can't be solved with leveling feet and rubber pads. If any of the following sound familiar, the issue is mechanical — and waiting will only make it worse:

  • Vibration started suddenly rather than gradually worsening over time
  • Loud banging during spin even with a properly balanced load
  • The machine has started "walking" across the floor despite leveling and pads
  • Water pooling under the machine after cycles — a sign hose connections have loosened
  • Grinding or rumbling sounds that have worsened over several months
  • Machine is 7+ years old with increasing vibration — bearing replacement vs. full replacement is a real cost conversation to have

If you're noticing grinding, persistent banging, or your machine has started moving across the floor, book a service call with My Appliance Repair before the problem graduates from a repair into a replacement — or worse, a flooded basement. Not sure where to start? Contact our team with a description of what you're hearing and we can often help you narrow it down before a technician even arrives.

Spring is a great time to address these issues as you're tackling home improvement projects after a long winter. Fall — when heavy comforters and guest bedding come out for washing — is when vibration problems tend to announce themselves loudly for the first time. Don't wait for the banging to get louder. Our technicians can diagnose whether you're dealing with a leveling issue, worn suspension components, or failing bearings, and give you an honest assessment of repair versus replacement costs before you commit to anything.

For Connecticut homeowners dealing with a washing machine that shakes, bangs, or walks across the floor, My Appliance Repair offers same-day service across the state. Schedule your repair online — we'll have your appliance running smoothly again fast.

title: Why Your Dryer Vent Is a Fire Waiting to Happen: Connecticut's Hidden Danger Every Homeowner Ignores
excerpt: Connecticut dryer vent fires are preventable. Learn the warning signs, seasonal risks, and when to call My Appliance Repair for a professional cleaning.
author: Elmir R.
content:
You clean the lint trap every time. Maybe you even wipe it down with a damp cloth occasionally. But here's the question most Connecticut homeowners can't answer: when did you last clean the vent duct running behind your dryer, through the wall, and out of your house? For many people, the honest answer is never. That duct is quietly accumulating lint, possibly harboring a bird nest, and — depending on your home's age and layout — it may be one blocked cycle away from a dryer vent fire.

This isn't meant to alarm you unnecessarily — it's a measurable, well-documented risk with a straightforward fix. But it does require action, and for Connecticut homeowners in particular, the risk is higher than most people realize.

The Scope of the Problem: What the Numbers Actually Say

According to the U.S. Fire Administration, clothes dryers cause approximately 2,900 home fires every year in the United States. The leading cause — responsible for 34% of those fires — is failure to clean. Not mechanical failure. Not faulty wiring. Lint buildup.

Here's why that matters: lint is extraordinarily combustible. It ignites at low temperatures and burns fast. And while your lint trap does its job on every load, it only captures roughly 75–80% of the lint your dryer produces. The rest migrates into the exhaust duct behind the machine. Over months and years, it coats the interior walls of the duct, narrows the airflow, and — especially in longer runs with bends and elbows — builds into a dense, dry, highly flammable mass sitting inches away from your dryer's heating element.

Cleaning the lint trap is necessary. It is not sufficient.

Why Connecticut Homes Face a Higher Dryer Vent Fire Risk

Connecticut's housing stock is older, denser, and more architecturally complex than the newer construction common in Sun Belt states. That creates specific dryer vent fire hazards that the team at My Appliance Repair sees regularly in homes across Fairfield, Hartford, and New Haven counties.

Longer, More Complicated Duct Runs

Cape Cods, colonials, and Victorians — the backbone of Connecticut's residential neighborhoods — frequently have dryers tucked into interior closets, back corners of basements, or second-floor laundry nooks. That means vent runs of 15 to 25 feet are common, often with multiple 90-degree elbows. Every elbow reduces airflow and creates a surface where lint catches and clumps. A duct that was never designed to modern standards and hasn't been cleaned in a decade is a serious fire hazard.

Winter Blockages

Connecticut winters are hard on exterior vent covers. Ice, frost, and packed snow can partially or fully block the exhaust flap, trapping heat and moisture inside the duct. That trapped moisture causes lint to clump and stick, accelerating buildup — and the trapped heat dramatically increases dryer vent fire risk during the very season when your dryer is working hardest.

Spring Nesting Season

Between March and May, birds and squirrels actively seek out exterior vent covers as nesting sites — especially covers with damaged or sticky flaps. A single full nest can block airflow entirely, causing a dryer to overheat within one drying cycle. If your vent cover hasn't been inspected after winter, there may already be nesting material inside it.

Summer Humidity

Connecticut's humid July and August weather means moisture in dryer exhaust air condenses more readily inside long duct runs. Rather than exhausting cleanly, lint gets wet, sticks to duct walls, and clumps. Homeowners often assume everything is fine during summer — low heating loads, windows open — but the duct may be accumulating buildup that becomes a hazard the moment fall laundry season kicks in.

Old Flexible Foil and Plastic Ductwork

Homes renovated in the 1980s and 1990s frequently had flexible accordion-style foil or plastic dryer ducts installed — at the time, a common and accepted practice. Those materials are now known to be fire hazards and are no longer up to code. They kink easily, trap lint in every ridge, and can ignite. Many Connecticut homes still have them running behind walls and under floors right now.

Warning Signs Your Dryer Vent Needs Attention

Your dryer will usually give you signals before a serious problem develops. If you notice any of the following, book a service call before the situation gets worse:

  • Clothes taking more than one cycle to fully dry — the most common early sign of restricted airflow
  • The dryer exterior or laundry room feeling unusually hot during a cycle
  • A burning smell during drying, even if faint or occasional
  • Lint accumulating on clothing after drying, or around the outside of the dryer
  • The dryer shutting off mid-cycle — this is the thermal overload protection triggering because the machine is overheating
  • Increased humidity or condensation building up in the laundry room
  • It has been more than 12 months since the duct was last professionally cleaned — or it has never been cleaned
  • You cannot remember when you last checked whether the exterior vent flap opens and closes freely

Any one of these signs warrants immediate attention. Multiple signs together mean the vent should be inspected today.

What a Proper Dryer Vent Cleaning Actually Involves

There's an important difference between cleaning the lint trap and cleaning the duct system. The lint trap is a 30-second task after every load. A full duct cleaning is a separate job entirely.

DIY Cleaning

For straight, accessible duct runs under 8 feet, a rotary vent cleaning brush kit — available at most hardware stores — can do a reasonable job. Disconnect the dryer from the duct, insert the flexible brush from the dryer end, and work your way through while vacuuming the loosened debris. Check the exterior vent cover from outside to confirm airflow is unobstructed when you're done.

Professional Duct Cleaning

For any run over 8 feet, runs with multiple elbows, or any situation where you suspect a blockage or haven't cleaned in years, professional service is the right call. A technician uses a rotary brush system combined with high-powered vacuum extraction to clear the entire run — from the dryer connection to the exterior, including sections completely inaccessible from the laundry room. My Appliance Repair technicians recommend scheduling this as part of your annual fall maintenance, alongside furnace servicing, before heavy dryer use resumes.

Exterior Vent Inspection

The exterior cover deserves its own check. The flap should open freely with light exhaust pressure and close fully when the dryer is off. Remove any nest material, debris, or ice damage. One important note: covers with fine mesh screens trap lint rapidly and should be replaced with a proper louvered cover — mesh is not a safe choice for dryer vents.

For average households, annual professional cleaning is the standard recommendation. Households with pets or large families doing heavy laundry loads should consider cleaning every six months, since pet hair significantly accelerates lint accumulation.

How to Know If Your Duct Is the Right Material

Even a recently cleaned duct can be a dryer vent fire hazard if it's made of the wrong material. Here's a quick guide to what you may find behind your dryer — and what to do about it:

  • Rigid metal duct (aluminum or galvanized steel): The current code standard. Smooth interior walls resist lint buildup, withstand heat, and exhaust safely over longer runs. This is what you want.
  • Semi-rigid metal duct: Acceptable for short, accessible runs. Slightly more flexible than rigid duct, but still far safer than foil or plastic options.
  • Flexible foil accordion duct: No longer code-compliant for concealed runs. The ridged interior traps lint aggressively, and the material can ignite. Replace immediately if found behind walls or under floors.
  • Flexible plastic duct: The most dangerous option. Melts and burns readily. If your duct is white or gray plastic, it should be replaced before your next laundry load — not at your next convenience.

If you're not sure what type of duct you have, a technician can identify the material and condition during a service visit and advise on whether cleaning, repair, or full replacement is the right step.

When Cleaning Isn't Enough: Duct Replacement and Appliance Repair

If your duct is crushed, kinked, or made of plastic or accordion foil material, cleaning it isn't the answer — it needs to be replaced with rigid or semi-rigid metal duct, which is the current code standard and the only type that exhausts safely over longer runs.

If your dryer is still running hot, shutting off, or taking multiple cycles to dry even after the vent has been cleared, the problem may be inside the appliance itself. A failing heating element, a worn thermostat, or a blown thermal fuse can all produce symptoms that look identical to a vent blockage. A dryer with persistent performance issues after a clean vent should be inspected by a repair technician before you write it off as needing replacement.

Quick tip: A $150 professional vent cleaning combined with a $200 appliance repair can extend your dryer's working life by five or more years — far more cost-effective than an $800–$1,200 replacement for a problem that was preventable.

If you're unsure whether your issue is the duct or the appliance, contact our team and we can help you figure out the right next step — a service visit covers both the appliance inspection and a ductwork assessment.

Quick Prevention Checklist for Connecticut Homeowners

  • Clean the lint trap after every single load — no exceptions, including light loads
  • Inspect the exterior vent cover every spring — check for ice damage from winter, debris, and nesting material from birds or squirrels
  • Schedule professional duct cleaning every 12 months — put it on your fall maintenance calendar alongside your furnace tune-up
  • Never run the dryer unattended — avoid running it when you leave the house or go to sleep
  • Replace flexible plastic or foil accordion duct now — not next year, not after the next cleaning
  • Know where your dryer's circuit breaker is — if you ever smell burning from the laundry room, cut power immediately and call for service

The Right Time to Act Is Before Heating Season

Late summer and early fall is the ideal window to deal with dryer vent maintenance. Back-to-school laundry, heavier fall bedding, and flannel everything means your dryer's workload is about to increase significantly. A vent that seemed to keep up through summer — lighter loads, more frequent short cycles — can fail quickly once you're running it hard in September and October. Getting ahead of it now, before you need the dryer daily, is exactly the right approach.
